title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives Election in Maryland's 8th Congressional District
description: Maryland's 8th Congressional District, which covers most of Montgomery County and parts of Carroll County, holds its 2026 general election on November 3, 2026. Incumbent Democrat Jamie Raskin, first elected in 2016 and a prominent figure on the House Judiciary Committee, is seeking re-election. The Democratic primary on June 23, 2026, features Raskin and three challengers, while four Republicans compete in their own primary for the chance to face the Democratic nominee. The district is considered safely Democratic in national forecasts, though the primary contests reflect internal party debates over the direction of the Democratic Party.
polling_note: No independent general-election polls were found for this race as of mid-June 2026. Ratings organizations such as Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball have not yet rated this specific district for 2026, but the 8th district has consistently voted Democratic in recent cycles.

candidates.name: Jamie Raskin
candidates.summary: Jamie Raskin is the incumbent U.S. Representative for Maryland's 8th Congressional District, first elected in 2016. He serves as the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and was previously a Maryland state senator and a constitutional law professor at American University's Washington College of Law. Raskin is a prominent progressive voice known for his roles in the January 6 investigation and impeachment proceedings against former President Trump.

candidates.name: J.D. Kumar
candidates.summary: J.D. Kumar is a finance executive and founder of MQAPITAL who is challenging incumbent Jamie Raskin in the Democratic primary. He holds bachelor's degrees in international finance, marketing, and Spanish from the University of Maryland and has studied at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Kumar has volunteered for past Democratic presidential campaigns and emphasizes pragmatic capitalism, immigration reform, and economic innovation.

candidates.name: Stephen Leon
candidates.summary: Stephen Leon is an intellectual property law specialist and entrepreneur running in the Democratic primary. He attended Northern Virginia Community College focusing on computer science and left early to found a company. Leon emphasizes balancing the federal budget through private sector climate technology investments, moderate immigration amnesty, and reforming the Democratic Party with data-driven decision-making.

candidates.name: Boris Velasquez
candidates.summary: Boris Velasquez is a national security technologist and former Marine Corps Sergeant running in the Democratic primary. He holds a Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence from Johns Hopkins University (candidate) and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science from George Mason University. Velasquez has worked for twelve years as a national security analyst across multiple administrations and frames his candidacy around class struggle, federal worker protections, and opposition to the influence of corporate donors in politics.

forecast.rationale: No general-election polling exists for this race as of mid-June 2026, and the general-election matchup is not yet set (the Democratic and Republican primaries are June 23, 2026, three days away). However, Maryland's 8th Congressional District is described as consistently Democratic in recent cycles and is considered safely Democratic in national characterizations. Incumbent Democrat Jamie Raskin is a well-established, high-profile officeholder first elected in 2016 and serves as the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee. The Republican field consists of four candidates with limited public profiles, none of whom completed the major local voter-guide questionnaire. The district's strong Democratic partisan lean, Raskin's incumbency and national prominence, and the comparatively low-profile Republican field all point to an overwhelming Democratic advantage in the general election. Confidence is medium rather than high because there are zero general-election polls and the general-election ballot is not yet determined.
